title: All hearts are under the control of the Most Compassionate

blocks.text: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) reported that he heard the Messenger of Allah (may Allah’s peace and blessings be upon him) say: “Indeed, the hearts of all the children of Adam are between two Fingers of the Most Compassionate, like one heart; He directs it as He wills.” Then the Messenger of Allah (may Allah’s peace and blessings be upon him) said: “O Allah, the Turner of the hearts, direct our hearts towards Your obedience”.

blocks.text: The Hadith therefore begins by telling us of Allah’s authority, then ends with a supplication that teaches us how to act on that knowledge. Whoever knows that their heart’s soundness and steadfastness are in their Lord’s hands turns to Him, rather than relying on themselves or on some good state they enjoyed in the past. Despite the Messenger’s exalted standing, and despite his past and future sins having been forgiven, he asked Allah to direct his heart to obedience. Everyone else is in even greater need of this. blocks.text: The hearts being between two Fingers does not imply physical contact or that Allah dwells within people’s bodies. In Arabic, saying that something is between two things does not require it to touch either of them. Allah says: “clouds which are held between the sky and the earth” [Al-Baqarah, 2:164] This does not mean that the clouds must touch the sky and the earth. Badr is described as being between Makkah and Madinah even though it is distant from both. A prayer barrier is described as being in front of the person praying—literally, in the Arabic expression, ‘between their two hands’—although it is separate from them. Sha‘ban can also be described as between Jumada and Dhu al-Qa‘dah without immediately adjoining either month. If such expressions do not require contact even when used of created things, we cannot impose a false meaning on a report about the Creator when the report does not indicate it.

 [2] Beware of rejecting the command of Allah when it comes to you, for Allah may not enable you to respond to his command afterward, as the hearts are between the two Fingers of Allah Who changes it as He wishes.

reading:
All hearts are under the control of the Most Compassionate

‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) reported that he heard the Messenger of Allah (may Allah’s peace and blessings be upon him) say: “Indeed, the hearts of all the children of Adam are between two Fingers of the Most Compassionate, like one heart; He directs it as He wills.” Then the Messenger of Allah (may Allah’s peace and blessings be upon him) said: “O Allah, the Turner of the hearts, direct our hearts towards Your obedience”.

Sahih Muslim, 2654

All human hearts, however many they are, however different their conditions, and whatever intentions and secrets they conceal, are under Allah’s authority as though they were one heart. No heart distracts Him from another, and none is beyond His control. Creating and resurrecting all people is likewise never beyond His power: “Your creation and resurrection is only like that of a single soul[1].” [Luqman, 31:28]

A person may struggle to put their own intention right, even though it is their own heart. They want to be sincere, but the desire for praise or money, or a sense of self-admiration, keeps returning. They may feel lonely and closed off inside, unable to dispel either feeling. Yet Allah can readily turn that heart from distress to openness, from heedlessness to awareness, and from misguidance to guidance.

The Hadith therefore begins by telling us of Allah’s authority, then ends with a supplication that teaches us how to act on that knowledge. Whoever knows that their heart’s soundness and steadfastness are in their Lord’s hands turns to Him, rather than relying on themselves or on some good state they enjoyed in the past. Despite the Messenger’s exalted standing, and despite his past and future sins having been forgiven, he asked Allah to direct his heart to obedience. Everyone else is in even greater need of this. Turning from obedience to disobedience, or from insight to blindness, is a calamity that deserves serious attention and fear.

The Hadith affirms Fingers as an attribute of Allah in a manner befitting His majesty, without likening them to created attributes, describing how they are, or denying them. The Arabic report specifies two Fingers among the Fingers of the Most Compassionate. The governing principle is: “There is nothing like unto Him[1], and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.” [Ash-Shura, 42:11] Just as we affirm His hearing and sight without making them like the hearing and sight of created beings, we affirm the attribute His Messenger has told us of while declaring Him free of any likeness to creation. Sharing a word does not mean sharing the same reality. Even among created things, a word’s meaning varies according to what it refers to: the Arabic word ra’s can refer to a person’s head, a mountain’s summit, or financial capital.

Regarding reports of this kind, Sufyan ibn ‘Uyaynah said: “They are just as they are, we affirm them and narrate them without asking how.” [Al-‘Uluw lil-‘Ali al-Ghaffar, pp. 156–158; English: Mountains of Knowledge, Inheritors of the Prophets, pp. 180–181]

The hearts being between two Fingers does not imply physical contact or that Allah dwells within people’s bodies. In Arabic, saying that something is between two things does not require it to touch either of them. Allah says: “clouds which are held between the sky and the earth” [Al-Baqarah, 2:164] This does not mean that the clouds must touch the sky and the earth. Badr is described as being between Makkah and Madinah even though it is distant from both. A prayer barrier is described as being in front of the person praying—literally, in the Arabic expression, ‘between their two hands’—although it is separate from them. Sha‘ban can also be described as between Jumada and Dhu al-Qa‘dah without immediately adjoining either month. If such expressions do not require contact even when used of created things, we cannot impose a false meaning on a report about the Creator when the report does not indicate it.

Ibn Qutaybah explained why interpreting the two Fingers as two blessings does not fit this context. If the point were simply that two blessings protect the heart, that alone would convey reassurance. Yet the report came in answer to fear and as evidence of our need to ask for steadfastness. Reports about the bearing of the heavens and the earth likewise bear on this point, as does Allah’s statement: “On the Day of Resurrection, the whole earth will be in His Grip, and the heavens will be rolled up in His Right Hand.” [Az-Zumar, 39:67] Here, belief in Allah’s attribute goes together with belief in His unrestricted control. Affirming either meaning does not dispense with affirming the other.

‘He directs it’ means that He turns the heart’s condition however He wills, easily and without anything preventing Him. Describing all these many hearts as one heart establishes the perfection of His power: the multitude of His creation does not burden Him. A point transmitted in al-Tibi’s commentary, in connection with the name ‘the Most Compassionate’, is that Allah’s care for people’s innermost affairs is part of His mercy. His knowledge of their secrets is therefore unlike created beings discovering one another’s secrets. A note below clarifies this transmission.

The Arabic word for ‘finger’ has ten recorded pronunciations. The most eloquent is iṣba‘, with an ‘i’ at the beginning and an ‘a’ after the ‘b’. This is an observation about the language in which the report was transmitted; it does not describe how the attribute is.

The supplication then asks Allah to direct our hearts in obedience to Him. As Ibn ‘Uthaymin explained, the Arabic preposition ‘ala conveys remaining within obedience as the heart turns from one good deed to another: from prayer to remembrance, from charity to fasting, from learning to other acts of goodness. The request is not merely for the heart to turn to obedience once and then leave it for disobedience.

This dependence on Allah calls for a prompt response to Him. Allah says: “O you who believe, respond to Allah and the Messenger when He calls you to what gives you life[1], and know that Allah comes between a person and his heart[2]” [Al-Anfal, 8:24] We must beware of rejecting a command when it first reaches us, then seeking guidance after a barrier has come between the heart and that guidance. Such fear should move us to hasten to obedience.

That is why those firmly grounded in knowledge ask: “Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate[1] after You have guided us, and grant us Your mercy; for You are the Munificent Bestower. [Al ‘Imran, 3:8] Among the Prophet’s supplications was: “O Allah, I seek refuge in Your might—there is no god but You—from You leading me astray.” [Sahih Muslim, 2717]

Allah has no need of His servants’ obedience. Their gratitude adds nothing to His self-sufficiency, and their disobedience diminishes nothing of it. Yet He does not approve of disbelief and does approve of gratitude: “If you disbelieve, then Allah is in no need of you, but He does not approve of disbelief for His slaves. If you are grateful, He approves that for you.” [Az-Zumar, 39:7] The benefit of guidance belongs to the servant, while the consequences of going astray fall upon them: “We have sent down to you the Book with the truth for all mankind. Whoever follows the guidance, it is to his own benefit, and whoever goes astray, it is only to his own loss. You are not a keeper over them.” [Az-Zumar, 39:41] Reverence for Allah’s power therefore opens the way to supplication, action and seeking His protection. It teaches the believer to keep asking for guidance and steadfastness until death.
